pages.title: Frostcap
pages.text: $(italic)Gelimyces nivalis.$() A pale fungus that glows faintly blue-white. From $(bold)Phase 3$(), wild patches appear on cold snow and ice, and it grows in shelves on the sides of Rimewood logs.$(br2)It needs no light and gives off no heat, so a cold-room farm is invisible to anything that hunts by warmth. The glow (light 3) is enough to find your way in the dark.

pages.title: Growing It
pages.text: Plant a Frozen Frostcap on $(bold)snow, ice or a Rimewood log$().$(br2)$(li)$(bold)-20°C or colder:$() ripens and spreads; twice as fast at -80°C$(li)$(bold)-20°C to 0°C:$() stalls$(li)$(bold)Above 0°C:$() dies$(br2)Like mushrooms, it stops spreading once five grow close together. A ripe cluster gives two or three caps.

pages.title: Keep It Frozen
pages.text: Harvested caps are $(bold)Frozen Frostcap$(): raw, safe, 2 hunger.$(br2)Carried above 0°C for about $(bold)5 minutes$(), they become $(bold)Thawed Frostcap$() (1 hunger), and 5 minutes later $(bold)Frostcap Mush$(), which you should not eat. Thawed caps never refreeze.$(br2)Caps in a chest keep as they are. Store the harvest in a cold room.
Three caps and a bowl: $(bold)6 hunger$(), and stew does not spoil.
Dry caps in a smoker or furnace for $(bold)Dried Frostcap$(): 3 hunger, stackable, and safe for long trips.

pages.title: ORSA Note
pages.text: $(italic)Specimen GN-7 is related to the genus Cryomyces, Antarctic rock fungi that survived eighteen months outside the International Space Station. ORSA notes it is not fussy about where it lives. ORSA notes it is not fussy about much at all.$()
